question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old woman presented to the pre-operative holding area this morning for an elective right total hip arthroplasty that the orthopedic team anticipates will last roughly two and a half hours under general anesthesia with spinal adjunct; the plan is for two to three nights of postoperative monitoring on the joint-replacement ward. Her hip pain has progressed over the past year to the point that, during the last week, she has required assistance for nearly every transfer from bed to chair and spends most of the day recumbent with pillows supporting the limb, venturing out of the room only for brief, guarded trips to the bathroom with a front-wheel walker. She states that aside from these short excursions, she has effectively remained in bed for the past four consecutive days. Of note, she is still within the first month of recovery from an open abdominal hysterectomy performed 27 days ago for symptomatic leiomyomata that failed medical management; that operation was uncomplicated, the midline incision now shows healthy granulation, and she has not experienced fever, wound drainage, or systemic infection since discharge. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exertional chest pressure, palpitations, or lower-limb tightness suggesting fluid overload, and an echocardiogram obtained last year for evaluation of palpitations showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction with normal valves. Respiratory history is unremarkable; she never smoked, uses no inhalers, and relates no episodes of wheeze, chronic cough, or oxygen dependence. Twenty years ago she was diagnosed with left-sided ulcerative colitis after colonoscopy with biopsy; flares have been infrequent and are well controlled on oral mesalamine 2.4 g daily, with her last course of prednisone more than five years ago. She has never required colectomy and denies current abdominal pain, tenesmus, or rectal bleeding. She explicitly recalls no episode of clots in the legs or lungs and has never undergone duplex ultrasonography or CT pulmonary angiography; her parents, siblings, and adult children are likewise free of unexplained venous events. She was exposed to unfractionated heparin during a prior cholecystectomy without any fall in platelet count, and outside records reveal normal coagulation studies and absence of antiphospholipid antibodies when these were checked by her gastroenterologist several years ago because of IBD. Chronic medications include mesalamine, acetaminophen-tramadol as needed for hip pain, and a daily calcium-vitamin D preparation; she takes no estrogens, selective estrogen receptor modulators, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents beyond 81 mg of aspirin, which was stopped five days ago per orthopedic protocol. She drinks wine socially on weekends, never used illicit drugs, and lives in a single-story home with her spouse, who has been helping her bathe and dress since the hysterectomy. On examination she lies supine on the stretcher, appears comfortable, and converses easily. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 124/68 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. Heart sounds are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and jugular venous contour is not elevated. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout with good air entry. The abdomen is flat with a well-healed 12-cm midline scar that is dry, non-erythematous, and non-tender; no hepatosplenomegaly is appreciated, and bowel sounds are present. Inspection of the lower limbs shows a network of bluish, tortuous superficial veins coursing along the medial aspect of both calves and behind the knees, more apparent when the legs are placed in the dependent position; there is no pitting edema, calf tenderness, or asymmetry of circumference, and the skin is warm with normal color. Pedal pulses are 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill is brisk, and there is full passive range of motion at the ankle. Neurologic examination demonstrates intact light-touch sensation and 5/5 strength about the contralateral hip and both knees, though active movement of the operative hip is limited by pain. No indwelling central venous catheters, ports, or peripherally inserted central lines are present; intravenous access today consists of a single 18-gauge cannula in the dorsal hand placed by nursing without difficulty. Recent laboratory values obtained two hours ago reveal hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 38 %, platelet count 243 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.1 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, AST 20 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, and baseline coagulation parameters of PT 12.4 s with an INR of 1.0 and aPTT 29 s. Electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min with no acute ST-T changes, and a chest radiograph obtained last week as part of the hysterectomy follow-up was clear. Airway assessment demonstrates Mallampati class II with adequate thyromental distance and neck mobility. She has been fasting since midnight and has voided without issue. Sequential compression sleeves are in place but have been intermittent because she finds the pneumatic cycle uncomfortable; pharmacologic prophylaxis has not yet been administered pending anesthesia induction.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds points for distinct perioperative risk factors:
- Age 62 (61–74 years): 2 points.
- Elective total hip arthroplasty: 5 points. Do not also count the same procedure as surgery lasting >45 minutes.
- Bed confinement for four consecutive days except for brief bathroom trips (>72 hours): 2 points.
- Separate major surgery within the past month (open hysterectomy 27 days ago): 1 point.
- History of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis), even though currently controlled: 1 point.
- Visible varicose veins in both calves: 1 point total.
Sum: 2 + 5 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 12.
Final answer: 12
